transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A small bakery in Portland, Oregon, that operates entirely on a "pay-what-you-can" model is celebrating its fifth anniversary this month, having served over 200,000 meals to community members since opening. The bakery, called "Rise Up," offers a full menu of breads, pastries, sandwiches, and soups with no set prices; customers are asked to pay what they can afford, and those who cannot pay are welcome to eat for free or volunteer an hour of work in exchange for a meal. Founder Maria Gonzalez says she was inspired to start the business after witnessing food insecurity in her neighborhood following the 2008 recession. Approximately 60 percent of customers pay the suggested donation or more, which allows the bakery to cover its costs and serve those who cannot pay. Local restaurants and grocery stores also donate surplus ingredients daily, reducing food waste while keeping the bakery's operating costs low. Rise Up has become so successful that organizers are planning to open a second location in Seattle next year, and they have created a free guide to help other communities start similar pay-what-you-can restaurants. Community members say the bakery has not only provided food but also created a welcoming space where people from all economic backgrounds can gather and connect.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The European Space Agency has successfully tested a new satellite navigation technology that could significantly improve location accuracy for smartphones and self-driving cars, even in dense urban areas where GPS signals often become blocked or unreliable. The new system, which uses a network of low-earth orbit satellites combined with advanced signal processing algorithms, can pinpoint locations to within 30 centimeters, compared to the current 5 to 10 meters with standard GPS. During a three-month pilot test in central London, delivery companies using the improved navigation reported a 40 percent reduction in delivery delays and a 25 percent decrease in fuel consumption. The technology also works indoors in many cases, allowing emergency responders to locate people inside buildings during fires or other crises. ESA officials say the system should be fully operational across Europe by 2028, with global coverage expected by 2032. The project has cost 2.3 billion euros so far, funded by contributions from ESA member states. Transportation experts believe the improved accuracy will accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous vehicles, which require highly precise location data to operate safely.
Questions 4 and 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
4. How accurate is the new navigation technology?
5. When is the system expected to be fully operational across Europe?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A new report from the American Library Association shows that public libraries in the United States are experiencing a major surge in popularity, with visits increasing by 22 percent over the past five years despite predictions that digital technology would make libraries obsolete. Far from declining, libraries have evolved to offer services that go far beyond book lending, including free high-speed internet access, job training workshops, 3D printing labs, maker spaces, free streaming services, and after-school programs for children. The report found that 98 percent of public libraries now offer free Wi-Fi, and nearly 70 percent provide digital literacy training for senior citizens. Library attendance for children's programs has increased by 35 percent since 2020, as parents seek out free, educational activities for their families. The report also notes that libraries serve as critical community resources during natural disasters and emergencies, providing shelter, power for charging devices, and access to critical information. Librarians say that while book borrowing remains steady, the expanded role of libraries as community hubs is driving the increase in visits. Many libraries are undergoing renovations to add more meeting spaces, study rooms, and technology centers to accommodate growing demand.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.

7. What percentage of public libraries offer free Wi-Fi?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Rachel): Hi David, did you manage to find a place to live for next year? I know you've been apartment hunting for weeks now—it sounds so stressful.

Man (David): It has been pretty stressful, actually. I looked at five places last week alone, and they all had problems. The first one was way too expensive—they wanted 1,200 pounds a month for a tiny studio that didn't even have a washing machine. The second was in a great location, right near campus, but the building was really noisy, and the landlord seemed terrible.
Woman: Oh, that's the worst. I heard so many horror stories about bad landlords when I was looking last year. Did you find anything promising?

Man: There was one place I really liked on Saturday—two-bedroom apartment in a quiet neighborhood, with a balcony and a real kitchen. The rent is 850 pounds per person per month, which includes all utilities. That's actually a pretty good deal for that area. But there's a catch—they need someone to move in by the 15th of next month, and I can't get out of my current lease until the end of the month.
Woman: Hmm, that is a problem. Could you talk to your current landlord about leaving early? Sometimes they're willing to let you go if you can find someone to take your room.

Man: I asked, and they said that's possible, but I'd have to find a replacement tenant myself and do all the viewings. That feels like a lot of work on top of my final exams next month. Also, the new apartment is on the third floor with no elevator, which might be annoying when I'm carrying groceries.
Woman: No elevator is a pain, but think of it as free exercise! What about the other people living there? Did you meet your potential roommate?

Man: Yeah, I met him when I viewed the place. He's a graduate student studying biology, seemed really quiet and responsible. He doesn't smoke or have parties, which is exactly what I want at this point—I'm too busy with my thesis for a noisy house. But I'm still hesitating because the deposit is a full month's rent, which I'd need to pay upfront.

Woman: Most places ask for a month's deposit, that's pretty standard. Look, I think you should go for it. Good affordable places that are quiet and near campus go really fast. You can probably find someone to take over your current room—put an ad up on the university housing page, I bet you'll get responses within a day or two. I found my replacement in less than 48 hours when I moved last year.
Man: You're probably right. I'll email the landlord tonight and say I'm interested. Fingers crossed it works out!

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Dr. Carter, Professor): Come in, Tyler! Have a seat. You wanted to talk about your research paper for American history? I've read your outline, and I think you've chosen a really fascinating topic.

Man (Tyler): Thanks, Professor Carter. Yeah, I wanted to talk to you because I'm having trouble narrowing down my focus. I'm writing about the Great Depression's impact on rural communities in the Midwest, but there's just so much information. I don't know how to structure it, and I'm worried I'm trying to cover too much.
Woman: That's a common challenge with historical research, especially for a 15-page paper. You're not writing a book—you need a clear argument. What specific question are you trying to answer?

Man: That's the problem. I was originally going to write about New Deal programs and whether they helped farmers, but then I found all these letters written by farm women during that period, and I got really interested in how women's roles changed as families struggled economically. Now I'm not sure which direction to take.

Woman: Why not combine them? There's actually been some excellent recent scholarship on how New Deal agricultural policies affected women differently than men. You could focus on how women's contributions to family income—through gardening, canning, taking in boarders, doing laundry for others—became essential for survival, yet were largely invisible in official relief programs.
Man: That sounds really interesting! But how do I make that a clear argument instead of just describing things?

Woman: A good structure would be to start with an introduction explaining your thesis—that New Deal farm policies were designed primarily around male farm owners and failed to recognize or support women's economic contributions. Then you could have a section on women's informal work, a section analyzing specific New Deal programs like the Agricultural Adjustment Act and why they didn't address women's needs, then a conclusion. I'd recommend looking at the Works Progress Administration's life histories collection—there are hundreds of interviews with rural women from that period available online through the Library of Congress.
Man: I didn't know about that collection. That would be perfect primary sources. What about citations? Should I use Chicago style?

Woman: Yes, please use footnotes in Chicago style, and make sure you're citing both primary sources and the secondary works I mentioned in your outline. Stop by during my office hours next week if you need help finding sources or refining your argument. This has the potential to be an excellent paper, Tyler.
Man: Thank you so much, Professor Carter. That gives me a much clearer direction. I really appreciate your help.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The human brain has a remarkable capacity known as "neuroplasticity"—the ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life. Contrary to the old belief that the brain becomes fixed and unchangeable after early childhood, modern neuroscience has demonstrated that our brains continue to create new pathways and alter existing ones in response to learning, experience, and even injury. This is the fundamental reason why people can recover abilities after strokes or brain injuries—other parts of the brain can learn to take over functions that were lost. But neuroplasticity isn't just relevant for recovery from injury; it explains how we learn any new skill at any age. When you practice a musical instrument, learn a new language, or even memorize information for a test, repeated activity strengthens the neural connections associated with that skill, making the task easier over time. This is why consistent practice is so much more effective than cramming—spaced repetition strengthens neural pathways far more effectively than one-time intense study. Research has also shown that activities requiring focused attention and novelty, such as learning to paint or studying a completely new subject, are particularly effective at maintaining brain health as we age. Physical exercise, especially aerobic exercise like walking or swimming, also supports neuroplasticity by increasing blood flow to the brain and promoting the production of growth factors that help new brain cells form. While it's true that children's brains are more plastic than adults', studies have found that adults retain significant capacity for change well into old age, especially if they remain mentally and physically active.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: The development of refrigeration technology in the late 19th and early 20th centuries transformed not just how people ate, but global trade, settlement patterns, and public health in ways that are rarely fully appreciated. Before mechanical refrigeration, people preserved food through methods like salting, smoking, pickling, drying, and canning. Fresh meat, dairy, fruits, and vegetables could only be transported short distances, which meant people's diets were highly seasonal and limited to what could be produced locally. Cities had to be supplied by nearby farms, and populations in warm climates had very restricted access to protein-rich foods that spoiled quickly. The first practical refrigerated rail cars were introduced in the 1870s in the United States, allowing beef from Texas and the Midwest to be shipped to eastern cities at a fraction of the previous cost. This dramatically lowered food prices, improved nutrition for urban workers, and reshaped the American meatpacking industry. By the early 1900s, refrigerated ships were carrying meat from Argentina and Australia to Europe, and fresh fruit from California and Florida to markets across the country. Home refrigerators, which became common in the 1920s and 1930s, changed domestic life completely, eliminating the need for daily shopping and the regular ice delivery that had been a feature of urban life. Refrigeration also made major contributions to public health by reducing foodborne illnesses caused by spoilage. Today, the cold chain—the refrigerated supply network that moves perishable goods from producer to consumer—is a critical part of the global food system, though it also raises environmental concerns due to energy use and refrigerants that contribute to climate change.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Silent book clubs, a growing international movement that began in 2012 in San Francisco, offer an alternative to traditional book clubs where members spend more time socializing than actually reading. In a silent book club, people gather at a designated location—often a café, library, bar, or park—bring whatever book they feel like reading, and spend about an hour reading silently together before having optional informal conversation about their books or anything else. There are no assigned books, no mandatory discussion questions, and no pressure to finish a particular title. The movement has spread rapidly because it addresses a common problem: many people love the idea of book clubs but either don't have time to read assigned books, dislike being put on the spot to discuss literature, or simply struggle to find quiet, uninterrupted reading time in their busy lives. Silent book clubs provide built-in distraction-free time that many participants say they would not prioritize on their own at home, where chores, screens, and family responsibilities constantly pull attention away. They also offer the low-pressure social benefit of being around other people who enjoy reading, without the anxiety that can come with formal literary discussion. Many chapters report extremely diverse attendance, including college students, working professionals, retired people, and parents with young children who use the reading time as a much-needed break. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many silent book clubs moved online, with members reading together over video calls while muted, a format that proved surprisingly popular and allowed isolated people to feel connected even while remaining physically separated. As of 2025, there are over 500 active silent book club chapters in more than 30 countries around the world.
